sources.entry: A news aggregator, also termed a feed aggregator, feed reader, news reader, RSS reader, is an application that aggregates web content such as newspapers/blogs/vlogs/podcasts in one location for easy viewing.

summary.name: RSS
summary.one_liner: RSS is an XML-based web feed format that lets users and applications track updates to websites in a standardized, machine-readable form, usually read through a news aggregator.
keywords: how to follow websites without social media
use_cases: Tracking many websites in one feed reader
Subscribing to blogs and news headlines
Getting website updates delivered to email
Automatically downloading new torrents via BitTorrent clients
Publishing frequently updated content from a website
summary.what_it_does:
RSS is a web feed format, specified as generic XML, that publishes a website's updates along with metadata such as publishing date and author. A news aggregator (feed reader) polls subscribed feeds and presents new items, so users do not have to check each site manually. The page describes several versions in two branches (RDF/RSS 1.* and RSS 2.*), with RSS 2.0 being the most widely used, and notes that extensions via XML namespaces allow features such as enclosures for podcasts. It also covers the history from the 1999 Netscape release through the Atom alternative and the 2005–2006 adoption of the orange feed icon.</what_it_does>

notable: Basis of podcast distribution, with enclosure support added in RSS 0.92 and RSS 2.0
Multiple versions (0.90 to 2.0.11) split into RDF and 2.* branches
Competing format Atom (RFC 4287) emerged from disputes over the RSS name and standard
Several browsers and readers dropped RSS support, while interest revived from the late 2010s
caveats: Google Reader, FeedDemon and Shiira were discontinued as of 2013 and Firefox 64.0 removed built-in RSS support
Some news aggregators do not support RSS files larger than 150KB (citation needed)
Several major sites such as Facebook and Twitter reduced or removed RSS feeds
